Digital healthcare cannot mean digital-only healthcare

What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps and online portals, access to care is becoming closely tied to access to technology.For many patients, digital healthcare can mean quicker consultations, easier access to medical records and fewer trips to hospitals. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.The problem is not simply whether a person owns a smartphone. Patients may struggle with internet connectivity, downloading and navigating apps, remembering passwords and OTPs, uploading documents or understanding information presented online.In many households, a single smartphone is shared by several family members, while caregivers often become the bridge between patients and digital health services.As government and private healthcare services increasingly encourage, and in some cases require, people to use digital platforms, a larger question is emerging: Is technology making healthcare more accessible, or creating a new barrier to accessing it?Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely.People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, receive medication and appointment reminders, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.Telemedicine became particularly important during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns made physical consultations difficult. But the experience also exposed how uneven access to digital healthcare could be.A DIG-EQUITY study published in, examining the experiences of people with diabetes, caregivers, healthcare providers, policymakers and community organisations in urban and rural Tamil Nadu, found significant differences in how people used digital health services.Younger patients were generally more comfortable with smartphones, health applications and teleconsultations, while many older people needed family members to book appointments, join consultations or access medical reports.For some, physical limitations added to the problem. Impaired vision or hearing, as well as difficulty handling smartphones, could make navigating digital platforms harder.Even among younger people, digital access did not automatically translate into a preference for online care. Some people with type 1 diabetes continued to prefer in-person consultations because of the need for physical examinations.The digital divide is also closely linked to where people live and what they can afford.Urban patients are more likely to have reliable internet connections, smartphones and access to digital services. A study published in, examining barriers to digital health transformation in India, found that the challenges went beyond simply having a smartphone or internet connection.The study identified poor network coverage and inadequate IT infrastructure, the high cost of devices and digital systems, a lack of technical expertise, language and communication barriers, and difficulties faced by users among the major challenges.For patients, these barriers can have very practical consequences. The study noted that some had to rely on family members' smartphones to attend teleconsultations, while the cost of smart devices could limit access to mobile health applications.The findings suggest that digital access cannot be measured simply by whether someone owns a phone. Reliable connectivity, affordability, digital skills, language accessibility and the availability of human support all influence whether a patient can actually use digital healthcare.That distinction becomes particularly important as healthcare services increasingly move online. Putting a service on a digital platform does not automatically make it accessible to everyone.India's digital health infrastructure is expanding rapidly. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), through platforms such as ABHA, is aimed at creating a connected digital health ecosystem, while eSanjeevani has widened access to telemedicine.With hundreds of millions of ABHA IDs created and telemedicine consultations running into hundreds of millions, the scale of this shift is significant.But the benefits of digital healthcare are not evenly experienced.The gap becomes particularly visible when digital systems are introduced at the hospital level. For some patients, the shift has not removed queues; it has created an additional one.Rekha (name changed), a patient at the Delhi National Cancer Institute, said patients earlier had to wait in a single OPD queue, with doctors arriving around 8am. According to her, the process now involves generating a token through the ABHA app before reaching the hospital, followed by another number at the reception.“Earlier there used to be only one OPD line and the doctors used to arrive at 8am. Now they have made it mandatory to download the ABHA app and apply for a token number. Then we get another number from reception, and doctors arrive at 10am. Several patients need immediate care, but this extra queue has made life a bit more difficult,” she said.For those without a smartphone or reliable internet connection, Rekha said the process can begin hours before they reach the doctor. Some patients, she said, arrive around midnight or 1am and spend the night waiting because they cannot access the network or generate a digital token.Those with smartphones may apply through the ABHA app around 5am and reach the hospital by 7am, she said, only to wait again at reception before seeing a doctor later in the morning.Dr Manisha Arora, Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said ABHA should remain a facilitator rather than become a gateway to treatment.“A patient should never feel that access to technology determines access to healthcare,” she said, noting that patients without an ABHA ID, smartphone or internet connectivity should continue to be able to register physically and receive the same clinical care.She stressed that hospitals should adopt a digital-first, not digital-only, approach.“That means retaining manual registration counters, providing assisted kiosks and having dedicated digital-support personnel, particularly for elderly and first-time users.”Digital insurance processes are another area where patients can struggle. Families dealing with hospitalisation may simultaneously have to navigate e-KYC, pre-authorisation, co-payments, deductions and non-payable items.Manivannan Selvaraj, Founder and Managing Director, Kauvery Group of Hospitals, said translating a clinical treatment plan into a pre-authorisation submission, and then managing the queries and follow-ups that come back, involves a long chain of steps that a patient is neither equipped nor educated to handle, and should not have to handle while they or a family member is unwell.“Sometimes delays or claim issues arise because documentation is incomplete rather than because of a medical concern,” Arora said, stressing that hospital insurance desks need to act as patient counsellors, explaining the process rather than merely uploading documents.“True digital accessibility is when technology works in the background and the patient still experiences a human interface at the front,” she said.At 65, Amarnath (name changed) has an insurance policy but says managing it digitally has become difficult. He is often unsure about when he can claim, when premiums are due and how to complete the process online, leaving his son to handle the details for him.“I have an insurance policy, but I often don’t know when I can make a claim, when the premium is due or how to complete these processes online. My son manages it for me. At my age, it is not always easy to visit a centre every time I need to check my policy or make a claim. If healthcare is becoming digital, these services should also be made accessible to elderly people, so that we can manage them ourselves without having to depend on others,” he said.He also highlighted how the growing use of digital payments in hospitals can create another challenge for elderly patients unfamiliar with the technology. Having a UPI-enabled phone does not necessarily mean being comfortable using it, particularly during a medical emergency when payments may need to be made quickly.“I have UPI on my phone, but for people of our generation, it is difficult to become fully comfortable with the process and make an immediate payment, especially during a health emergency. This is something that should also be addressed,” he said.The pandemic offered an early and stark example of how closely technology and healthcare had become intertwined.While telemedicine and digital systems helped patients access services during lockdowns, other parts of the healthcare chain showed that digitisation alone could not solve problems of capacity and access.As reported byearlier, delays in Covid testing became a major concern during the second wave. Udham Singh, 22, developed high fever, severe cough, body ache and breathlessness after his sample was collected for an RT-PCR test. His report, which confirmed Covid infection, came several days after the sample was taken.“I would have landed in an ICU had I waited for some more time. The element of uncertainty due to delay also caused extreme mental trauma,” Singh said.For patients waiting at home, the delay was not merely an inconvenience. It affected decisions about treatment and isolation. Some families also faced difficulties maintaining quarantine while waiting for test results.Priya Jaiswal, a resident of Old Delhi, recalled how a network outage during the pandemic left her dependent on officials for essential medicines. With her internet connection down, she could not use UPI to make payments or order medicines online, leaving her waiting for officials to arrive at her home.“We had to wait for hours for officials to arrive and hand over the medicines while we were in quarantine. Even online consultations became difficult because of continuous power cuts at a time when we needed healthcare the most,” she said.The surge in demand for Covid testing also put pressure on government laboratories to issue digital reports on time, highlighting another challenge for digital healthcare: a digital interface is only as effective as the system supporting it.Covid-19 vaccination certificates also affected people's travel and employment plans.Varghese Thomas, a youth from the city, told TOI that five people in his group had taken their first vaccine dose around the same time, but only one had received the certificate nearly 40 days later.“When we applied for jobs, prospective employers were asking us about the vaccination. They wanted us to produce the certificate,” he said.Registering through Co-WIN was another difficulty for people in rural areas.As reported byearlier, 68-year-old Adhi Kesavan from Gudiyattam in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district had to travel around 5-7 km with his wife to a common service centre to register for vaccination.Kesavan did not own a smartphone or know how to use one. He was directed to the centre by his panchayat head, who told him that his details could be registered there and that the hospital would contact him when a vaccine became available.“I heard from our panchayat head that we can get vaccinated if we register at the e-sevai maiyyam. Our number will be given to the hospitals nearby and we will get a call once the vaccine is ready,” Kesavan said.He was still waiting for that call.India's digital-health expansion will ultimately be measured not only by how many people are connected to the system, but also by whether those who are not can still access care with the same ease and dignity.The goal should not be to make healthcare digital at any cost. It should be to make healthcare more accessible, using technology when it helps, and providing human support when it doesn't.Because for a patient struggling to connect, navigate an app, remember an OTP or make a digital payment, the smartphone should never become another obstacle between them and a doctor.
Article Summary: Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely. Patients can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.

NEW DELHI: Govt has made biometric Aadhaar authentication mandatory for subsidised domestic LPG refills from Oct 1, reports Atul Mathur.The Union petroleum ministry said nearly 90% of consumers have already completed the authentication process. Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Saturday the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) India has signed with many countries are unlocking new opportunities for youths in fields ranging from entrepreneurship to jobs.Addressing a 'Rozgar Mela' virtually after distributing 51,000 appointment letters in govt sector to the recruits, he said these agreements pave the way for new partnerships and markets for entrepreneurs, while creating fresh career possibilities for the youth as well. "Our youth's talent and skills have earned global confidence and the world pins great hopes on our innovators, entrepreneurs, and our vibrant youth power," he said.With the Brics summit recently concluded, he said India's effort has been to ensure that the cooperation between these countries does not remain limited to govts alone. "Our entrepreneurs, farmers, women, youth - everyone should become an active partner in this partnership," he said, adding the country's burgeoning startup ecosystem reflects the youth power as it is no longer limited to big cities and has expanded to tier-2 and tier-3 cities as well."Today, India is world's third largest startup ecosystem. And our startup story is no longer just the story of big cities. Today, nearly half of recognised startups are in tier-2 and tier-3 cities," he added.Modi said the country is moving forward toward a very significant goal of building a developed India by 2047. "In this, young people have a significant role to play. While serving in govt, you must make every decision that continuously strengthens the campaign for a developed and self-reliant India. Being young, you have a special responsibility, particularly towards other young people," the PM added.
Article Summary: Prime minister narendra modi virtually addresses 'rozgar mela', jobs fair, from new delhi. Modi: free trade agreements (ftas) india has signed with many countries are unlocking new opportunities for youths. "our youth's talent and skills have earned global confidence," he said.

Article Title: ‘Bharat is not a geography, it is responsibility’: CDS Gen Subramani
Article Text:
He was addressing graduates at the IIT Roorkee convocation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that self-reliance (Atmanirbharta) is crucial for the progress of a nation? Strongly agree Strongly disagree 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani on Saturday said “as technology is changing, it is not the most brilliant person but the person who has the ability to adapt to changing circumstances, ability to learn, and ability to change with the times will succeed”. Addressing graduates at the IIT Roorkee convocation, the CDS said “Bharat is not a geography. It is a responsibility which generations before you have carried, and you will carry as you navigate this world.”Explaining the meaning of ‘BHARAT’, Gen Subramani said, 'B' stands for build. Be a builder, don't just be a technology consumer; be a technology creator; 'H' stands for harness, harness the power of technology, the power of AI, the power of space, the power of your intelligence, and harness the power of your teams; 'A' stands for adaptability, which I have already spoken about, adapt to the world, adapt to changing circumstances; 'R' stands for research, research must have outcomes. It has to be related to what the country requires; and 'A stands for Atmanirbharta (self-reliance).”Explaining the last alphabet in BHARAT, Gen Subramani said, “'T' stands for taking responsibility. Take responsibility for yourself, take responsibility for your actions, and take responsibility to contribute, even in a small measure, to take our nation forward.”“If each one of us contributes like the droplets of a river, the nation will continue to move forward, grow, and achieve the dream of Viksit Bharat 2047," he told students.He urged future engineers and technologists to focus on developing resilient systems.The CDS also introduced the acronym “DHARA” to describe the transformations shaping the world. “I want to speak about the changing world, and I'll give you an acronym for that. That is Dhara. What I mean by Dhara is D - disruptive; H - hyper-connectedness; A - asymmetry; R - realignment; and A - autonomy.”“The world is undergoing enormous disruption. Technology is changing faster than we can catch up. You, as graduates, will have to learn, unlearn, relearn, adapt, and remain curious throughout if you want to keep up with the changing world,” Gen Subramani said.
Article Summary: Chief of defence staff (cds) general ns raja subramani on saturday said ‘as technology is changing, it is not the most brilliant person but the person who has the ability to adapt to changing circumstances’ he was addressing graduates at the iit roorkee convocation.

Article Title: NSE IPO Day 2: After 43% subscription on first day, GMP stands at 8%; what brokerages are saying
Article Text:
The IPO is an offer for sale (OFS) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that NSE will not receive any money raised through the issue.

NSE IPO subscription status

Retail Individual Investors (RIIs) subscribed to 44% of the 4.41 crore shares reserved for them.

Non-Institutional Investors (NIIs) subscribed to 72% of the 1.89 crore shares allocated to the category.

Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) subscribed to 19% of the 2.52 crore shares reserved for them.

NSE IPO GMP today

NSE IPO: What brokerages are saying

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

NSE IPO Day 2: National Stock Exchange of India IPO, India’s second largest till date, enters its second day of subscription with a grey market premium (GMP) of around 8%, pointing to expectations of a moderate gain when the shares list.On the first day, the issue was subscribed 43% overall, with bids received against the 8.86 crore shares on offer. Retail investors subscribed to 44% of the 4.41 crore shares reserved for them.The IPO is an offer for sale (OFS) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that NSE will not receive any money raised through the issue. The proceeds will go to the existing shareholders selling their stakes. The price band has been set at Rs 1,700-1,785 per share, with a lot size of eight shares.Also Read | NSE IPO: Why did India's second largest initial public offering not get fully subscribed on Day 1? At the upper end of the price band, a retail investor will need to invest a minimum of Rs 14,280 to bid for the subscription. The post-issue market capitalisation is estimated at around Rs 4,41,788 crore. The issue closes on September 21, while the shares are expected to be listed on BSE on September 24.Demand remained steady on the first day, with the IPO receiving subscriptions for 43% of the 8.86 crore shares on offer.The NSE IPO is commanding a grey market premium of around Rs 142, or 8%, over the upper end of its Rs 1,785 price band. Based on this GMP, the implied listing price is around Rs 1,927 per share, indicating expectations of a moderate listing gain.Brokerages have largely taken a positive view of the National Stock Exchange’s IPO. Thomas J. Priju, Portfolio Manager, Karma Capital sees NSE as a structural growth story, underpinned by the continued evolution of India's capital markets.“In our view, the exchange has the potential to emerge as a steady compounder over the long term and can be a meaningful long-term holding in a portfolio. In the near term, a resolution of the issues around the new closing auction mechanism (CAS) could provide an additional catalyst for the stock. Over a much longer horizon, as NSE's role in India's financial markets continues to deepen, the business is likely to command a valuation multiple more akin to that of a public utility,” he says.Also Read | NSE IPO opens for subscription: From GMP, market cap to status & global comparison - top 10 things to know He also believes that there could be some selling on the listing day as certain pre-IPO investors, including eligible AIFs, can monetise their holdings.“Other pre-IPO shareholders remain subject to a six-month lock-in period. This could create some temporary supply and provide a buying opportunity for long-term investors. The IPO saw 43% subscription on the first day, with institutional participation relatively muted at this stage. Given that QIB participation typically builds towards the end of the issue period, we would expect subscription levels to strengthen as the IPO progresses,” he adds.Analysts point to NSE’s market leadership, strong margins, debt-free balance sheet and expanding investor base as factors supporting the long-term investment case. They also see the IPO as an opportunity to gain exposure to India’s dominant market infrastructure company.However, the valuation remains a consideration. At 42.9 times FY26 earnings, the issue is not inexpensive, while NSE’s earnings are closely linked to trading activity, particularly options. A GMP of 8% indicates positive demand, but does not suggest excessive enthusiasm.
Article Summary: The ipo is an offer for sale (ofs) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that nse will not receive any money raised through the issue. The post-issue market capitalisation is estimated at around rs 4,41,788 crore. The issue closes on september 21, while the shares are expected to be listed on bse on september 24.

Article Title: Bill Gates said his children will inherit ‘less than 1%’ of his wealth; ex-wife Melinda Gates is making sure of it, reveals why she didn’t fund daughter's startup
Article Text:
Bill Gates said his children will inherit ‘less than 1%’ of his wealth; ex-wife Melinda Gates is making sure of it, reveals why she didn’t fund daughter's startup

Why Melinda French Gates did not fund her daughter’s startup

Bill Gates said his children will inherit less than 1%

Bill Gates daughter Phoebe launched Phia shopping app

Melinda French Gates says rejection can help female founders

Bill Gates has said his children will inherit less than 1% of his wealth when he dies, and his ex-wife Melinda French Gates appears to be following a similar approach when it comes to helping their children build careers. In a 2025 interview, French Gates revealed that she deliberately stayed out of her daughter Phoebe Gates’ startup fundraising, even though she could have easily opened doors through her vast network. Instead, she watched from the sidelines as her daughter tried to raise money from investors. “She got capitalized not because of my contacts, not because of me. I wouldn’t put money into it,” French Gates said. Her reason was simple: if the startup was a real business, she wanted other investors to believe in it too.French Gates discussed the decision at the Power of Women’s Sports Summit last year, where she explained why she chose not to invest in her daughter’s company.“She got capitalized not because of my contacts, not because of me. I wouldn’t put money into it,” she said.French Gates said she wanted her daughter to experience the fundraising process herself, including the possibility of being rejected by investors.“If this is a real business,” she said, others should be willing to back it.“That’s what I told her,” French Gates added. “She’s growing from this.”Melinda French Gates’ approach echoes a decision Bill Gates has spoken about in the past. The Microsoft cofounder has said his children will receive less than 1% of his fortune after his death. Gates has argued that giving children an extremely large inheritance would not necessarily be helpful and that they should make their own way.French Gates' decision not to invest directly in her daughter's company follows a similar principle. Rather than using her own wealth or contacts to help secure funding, she wanted her daughter to build the company independently.Bill Gates’ youngest daughter Phoebe Gates, has launched a fashion-tech startup called Phia with her Stanford roommate, Sophia Kianni. Phia is a platform that compares clothing prices across more than 40,000 websites, allowing shoppers to search for deals.In April 2025, Phoebe Gates, who was then 22, said her parents had not allowed her to leave Stanford to build a startup, despite her father having taken a different path when he launched Microsoft.The startup has since attracted attention, including recent scrutiny over claims about sales attributed to the platform.For French Gates, the decision was also connected to the challenges faced by women building companies. “It is very, very hard to get your business funded if you’re a woman,” she said. “And so you do have to learn a bit how to have the courage to play the game and to stick with it.”French Gates said resilience is a common quality among successful women featured on her YouTube series, Moments That Make Us.“I saw that going through something difficult changed all of them, and that they had to learn to find resilience somewhere,” she said. “And in finding that resilience, they found themselves.”
Article Summary: Melinda french gates said she deliberately stayed out of her daughter phoebe gates’ startup fundraising. She said she wanted her daughter to experience the fundraising process herself, including the possibility of being rejected by investors. French gates' decision not to invest directly in her daughter's company follows a similar principle.

Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O' Leary: Follow this rule, and you will be a millionaire when you retire
Article Text:
How Kevin O’Leary’s 15% savings rule works

Why saving 15% can be difficult for average workers

What a $68,000 salary looks like after basic expenses

How Warren Buffett’s advice compares

Kevin O’Leary has suggested a simple rule for Americans looking to build a seven-figure retirement portfolio. The Shark Tank US judge has recommended saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time. For someone earning $68,000 a year, the investor says consistently following that approach could result in a millionaire-sized retirement portfolio by age 65. The Canadian investor and entrepreneur recently shared the advice in an Instagram post, telling people to put money into the market rather than spend it on things they do not need. His calculation assumes decades of consistent investing and relies on long-term stock market growth.“What piece of advice do I give my kids over and over and over again about money? Don't spend it. Save it, invest it, let it compound. That's the gift the market gives you. Take 15% of all your paycheques, all your side hustle, any cash Granny gives you, put it in the market, and just let it compound. If you make $68,000 a year, the average salary, and you do this your entire life, just 15% of your paycheque- you'll end up a millionaire by retirement in '65.Best piece of advice I can give anybody. Don't buy stuff you don't need; invest it instead. Cheers,” O’Leary said in the post.By his example of an income of $68,000, that would mean a 15 per cent contribution of roughly $10,200 a year, or $850 a month. If you invested that amount consistently for 40 years, from age 25 to 65, your portfolio could grow substantially with compound returns.The strategy is straightforward on paper, but putting aside 15% of income can be difficult for households already dealing with rent, food, student loans and other living costs.The calculation depends heavily on investment returns and how long the money stays invested. Assuming an average annual return of about 10%, broadly in line with the S&P 500's historical long-term average, investing $850 every month for 40 years would produce approximately $5.3 million.At a lower assumed average return of 7 per cent, that same monthly contribution would have accumulated to about $2.2 million over four decades. In either case, the investor would have more than $1 million at retirement. Remember that actual investment returns can vary from year to year and are not guaranteed.So O’Leary’s estimate is an illustration of long-term compounding rather than a guaranteed outcome. It also assumes the worker can contribute uninterrupted over a 40-year career.The challenge is less about the arithmetic than whether an average household can consistently set aside that much money. Workers earning between $50,000 and $79,999 are among those most likely to report falling behind on retirement savings, with 55% saying they feel behind.According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the personal savings rate was 4.4% of disposable income in mid-2025, a Fortune report noted. For a $68,000 earner, that would be about $3,000 a year, a far cry from the $10,200 annual investment suggested by O’Leary’s 15% rule.Vanguard data also show that the median total contribution rate among 401(k) participants, including employee and employer contributions, is about 11.5%. That figure applies mainly to workers with access to a 401(k), so it does not represent the entire workforce.An American household making $68,000 before taxes will take home about $52,000 to $54,000 after federal and state taxes. This will leave about $3,600 a month for other expenses.Average US rent is about $1,740 a month, according to RentCafe. That would leave around $1,860 before other household costs. Groceries can add as much as $400 a month for a single person based on Bureau of Labour Statistics data, reducing the amount further.The remaining amount could drop to around $726 with student loan payments averaging about $434 a month and utilities at about $300. That would mean that saving $850 a month would be more than what you would have left after all of the expenses above.Even if the calculation is based on 15% of take-home income rather than gross pay, the target is still substantial. Nearly $52,000 in annual take-home income is about $650 a month at 15 per cent, which might still leave only about $150 in discretionary income under the expense assumptions.O’Leary agrees with Buffett’s long-term, low-cost approach to investing. Buffett has said that on the whole, average investors are better off with low-cost S&P 500 index funds than paying high fees to professional managers.“Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard’s),” Buffett wrote in a 2013 shareholders’ letter. “I believe the trust’s long-term results from this policy.”
Article Summary: Kevin o’leary has suggested a simple rule for americans looking to build a seven-figure retirement portfolio. Shark tank us judge has recommended saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang rejects Dario Amodei and Sam Altman’s 'AI will kill us all warnings': ‘Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to…’
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang says ‘no’ to 2030 extinction threat

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has outrightly rejected the apocalyptic claims that artificial intelligence (AI) will cause the extinction of humanity in the coming years, dismissing such warnings as baseless and exaggerated scare tactics. Speaking with CBS News, Huang challenged these ‘doomsday predictions’ voiced by prominent tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, cautioning the public and lawmakers not to be misled by panic.“Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist," Huang stated in an interview, adding, “Read between the lines. They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that that's a problem. We have plenty of laws, so let's apply those first.”Huang’s comments follow a heated public dispute triggered earlier this month by Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic. Coxon posted on social media that developers of frontier AI models believe the technology could wipe out humanity before the decade concludes.This ignited widespread controversy and prompted Amodei, Altman and Elon Musk to urge a deliberate slow down in model development.Huang flatly rejected those forecasts, arguing they have no grounding in scientific reality.“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,” Huang added.As the biggest producer of specialised chips powering AI models developed by OpenAI and competing labs, Nvidia holds an immense financial stake in the conversation. Soaring demand for its graphics processors has driven the company's valuation to $5.3 trillion, solidifying its rank as the world's most valuable enterprise.When asked why the public should accept his safety assurances given Nvidia’s obvious financial motives, Huang maintained that corporate health depends entirely on dependable technology.“Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services. If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished,” he noted.Huang also said that current American frameworks dealing with unauthorised computer access, damage liabilities and product safety are more than adequate.
Article Summary: Jensen huang rejects apocalyptic claims that artificial intelligence will wipe out humanity in the coming years. ‘2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to happen. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,’ he said.

Article Title: Anthropic, CEO of which called for slowing AI development, may release new model ahead of IPO
Article Text:
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra shakes up enterprise spending

Anthropic is reportedly weighing the release of a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to counter the rising momentum of rival OpenAI’s newly deployed GPT-6 Astra, a report has said, citing three people familiar with internal discussions. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (IPO) and arrives two weeks after Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei released a 3,800-word essay urging the global AI ecosystem to curb the speed of frontier model releases out of concern for systemic safety risks.As per a report by news agency Reuters, the internal push to deploy a countermeasure highlights the fierce commercial rivalry between the two frontier developers. Amodei warned of dark scenarios involving swarms of autonomous AI agents hacking websites without human oversight. This stance received public backing from OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceX head Elon Musk.Now, Anthropic finds itself balancing those cautionary declarations against intense market pressure, with internal teams evaluating the safety benchmarks of its next system while deliberating whether to greenlight a launch, the report noted.OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 Astra on September 3, highlighting significant leaps in autonomous computer use, coding, professional workplace tools and cybersecurity. The launch has reportedly seen rapid adoption across corporate clients. Data tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp shows GPT-6 Astra capturing approximately 13% of monitored enterprise AI expenditures, compared to roughly 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable.Despite OpenAI's recent gains, several current backers and funds preparing to invest in both upcoming IPOs argue that Astra does not present an existential threat to Anthropic. Analysts point to the considerable time it takes for corporate clients to rip out and replace entrenched software vendors.Furthermore, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate climbed past $65 billion by late July, surging from approximately $9 billion at the close of 2025. In comparison, OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate crossed $40 billion in July.Beyond its direct duel with OpenAI, Anthropic faces broader structural challenges across the industry. For example, the rapid rise of open-source and open-weight alternatives from China gives businesses cheaper pathways to build internal infrastructure without paying premium token fees to proprietary providers.Major customers are also looking inward. Meta Platforms, historically one of Anthropic’s top enterprise accounts, is actively looking to scale back its reliance on Claude systems as it expands its own internal computing models.
Article Summary: Openai’s gpt-6 astra shakes up enterprise spending on ai. Anthropic ceo dario amodei released a 3,800-word essay urging the global ai ecosystem to curb the speed of frontier model releases. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (ipo)

Article Title: Days after Michael Dell briefly became world’s second richest man, he is selling 4,100-sq-ft Boston penthouse that he purchased 10 years ago for $10.9 million
Article Text:
Michael Dell’s almost untouched luxury home

Could buyers land a bargain

Not Michael Dell's first headline-making property deal

Just days after Michael Dell briefly climbed to the position of the world’s second-richest man, the Dell Technologies founder is making headlines again — this time in real estate. Dell has put his 4,100-square-foot Boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. Located in Boston’s Millennium Tower, the penthouse offers sweeping city views, luxury finishes, and access to exclusive amenities. The residence reflects Dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in Texas and Hawaii. The listing comes amid Dell’s extraordinary financial year, with his net worth surging by more than $80 billion thanks to booming demand for AI infrastructure.Dell bought the Millennium Tower penthouse in 2016 through an LLC. Nearly a decade later, the roughly 4,100-square-foot, three-bedroom unit is heading to a sealed-bid auction with a reserve price $4.4 million below what he originally paid — a potential 41% discount from its last sale price.Bidding is open now and closes on October 29, though the property remains subject to a prior sale.Perched on the 59th floor of Millennium Tower, the penthouse comes with sweeping views and, according to the listing agent, has barely been lived in since Dell bought it. Notably, the home's oven has apparently never even been turned on.The sale comes at an interesting moment for Dell. His fortune took a $15.1 billion hit this past week as Dell Technologies shares fell amid a broader AI-stock selloff, knocking him down to No. 4 on Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires List. Just days earlier, he had briefly climbed to No. 2 on that same list for the first time. Despite the sharp drop, there's little to suggest the sale is driven by financial necessity — Dell remains one of the wealthiest people in the world.The auction is being handled by Paramount Realty USA in collaboration with SERHANT. Massachusetts. Paramount founder and CEO Misha Haghani acknowledged there's a real possibility a buyer could land a good deal, though he was careful to note that what counts as a "good deal" is ultimately subjective and will come down to how the market responds. Haghani declined to comment on why Dell is selling.This isn't Dell's first eye-catching real estate move. The Dell Technologies founder and CEO previously paid $100.47 million for a penthouse at Manhattan's One57 in 2014, a deal that set records at the time. His willingness to buy — and now sell — trophy properties at steep prices underscores a pattern of high-profile real estate bets that mirror the volatility of his tech fortune, which has swung dramatically in recent weeks alongside the broader AI-driven market turbulence hitting Dell Technologies stock.
Article Summary: Michael dell has put his 4,100-square-foot boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. The residence reflects dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in texas and hawaii.

Article Title: Oracle layoffs reach Abilene, the 'flagship' Stargate data center that Oracle keeps showing as proof the OpenAI deal is fine: Employee says he found out he was fired when...
Article Text:
Oracle employees lost Slack and VPN before the layoff email reached them

Abilene shows what Oracle's AI buildout costs on both sides of the ledger

Oracle's layoffs on September 14 reached Abilene, Texas, the site the company has spent months holding up as evidence that its OpenAI partnership is on track. One employee there, an IC2 in OCI who says he joined on February 2, described the morning on r/employeesOfOracle: the termination email arrived at 5am Central, he did not see it, and he only realised what had happened when his badge failed at the gate. His Slack was already locked. His last performance review had been "meets expectations". Another poster in the same thread said Customer Hardware Support was cut at Abilene, Phoenix and Ashburn.Abilene is not an incidental site. It is the flagship Stargate campus, the one Oracle cites when it talks about 200MW of operational capacity and an eight-building build running on schedule. It is also the site OpenAI has decided not to expand, preferring clusters with newer Nvidia chips, and the one lenders declined to finance with Oracle as tenant. Oracle does not own it. It leases the facility from Crusoe on a 15-year deal worth more than a billion dollars a year. Oracle has not commented on the cuts.The sequence was the same everywhere. Federated logins stopped working around 4am Eastern, Slack sessions dropped out between 5am and 5.30am, and the email from "Oracle Leadership" landed at 6am. Several people on the subreddit said they were locked out before they could read it.One OCI employee wrote that his login let him in for a second, then booted him out. Another found out from a text sent by a coworker while he was walking home from a run.The posts ran through the morning across OCI security, CI/CD, enterprise engineering, observability, executive escalations, Fusion, NetSuite sales, Customer Success Services, Oracle Health, EPM, HR Technology and data centre compliance. Employees tracked the Slack member count as it fell, putting the US drop at roughly 3,200 against Friday.Oracle severance works out to 4 weeks plus a week for every year servedOracle is offering four weeks of base salary plus one additional week per year of service. The March version of the plan capped the total at 26 weeks. The latest documents do not state a cap.That formula explains the numbers circulating on Reddit. A data centre technician with eight months reported four weeks. Someone with four years in the database org got seven and called it a kick in the nuts. An IC5 with 7.5 years got ten. By comparison, Salesforce's standard policy runs up to 30 weeks and Microsoft offered up to 39 weeks this summer.The money behind Abilene is what makes the cuts there awkward. Oracle reported $28.5 billion in first-quarter capital expenditure, against $8.5 billion a year earlier, and kept its fiscal 2027 forecast at $90 billion to $95 billion. It raised its restructuring plan by about $700 million on Friday, to roughly $2.8 billion, and tied part of that to AI adoption across some functions.Headcount had already fallen by 21,000 in the year to May 31, leaving about 141,000 staff before September 14. One employee on the subreddit, writing from Abilene, put it more plainly than any filing: he had previously worked at IBM and Microsoft, so he would be fine, he just had to get out of town first.
Article Summary: Oracle employees lost slack and vpn before the layoff email reached them on september 14. The termination email arrived at 5am central, he did not see it, and he only realised what had happened when his badge failed at the gate. Customer hardware support was cut at abilene, phoenix and ashburn.

Article Title: Apple executive reveals why he hates screen protectors: It makes my skin crawl because …
Article Text:
Apple executive reveals why he hates screen protectors: It makes my skin crawl because …

Apple wants iPhone screens to last longer

Apple says it tests screens for years of use

Many iPhone users put a screen protector on their phones as soon as they take them out of the box. But one Apple executive has admitted that seeing a screen protector on an iPhone is not something he likes. Tom Marieb, Apple ’s vice president of hardware engineering (the role that current CEO John Ternus once held), explained why during a recent group interview while discussing the company’s latest work on display durability. “Personally, when I see someone put a screen protector on their iPhone, it makes my skin crawl, because we work so hard to make beautiful front screens,” Marieb said.Tom Marieb said Apple has been working on new coatings that can protect the display from scratches while also making the surface resistant to wear over time. The two goals can be difficult to achieve together, he explained.“We worry about scratching, which is obviously very dependent on having [material that can withstand] very sharp things going into the screen. But we also worry about wear over time; as people use the screen, whether they’ll wear away that surface.”According to Marieb, Apple tried to find a balance between scratch resistance and long-term durability with Ceramic Shield 2.“We could have made it more scratch-resistant, but it would have been a little less wear-resistant. It’s the long life we’re looking for against both of those loads over time.”Apple's approach is not simply to test how a screen performs when it is new. Tom Marieb said the company tries to recreate how people actually use their phones in everyday life. “We very much try to meet the customer where they live,” he said.Apple also uses accelerated testing to simulate years of use in a much shorter period. Marieb said the company can represent five years of use, or even more, within a couple of weeks of testing.“And as you said, people waiting a year or two to actually see the benefits of [Ceramic Shield 2] means we've correctly predicted how people would use it,” he said.
Article Summary: Apple executive reveals why he hates screen protectors: it makes my skin crawl. Tom marieb said apple has been working on new coatings that can protect the display from scratches while also making the surface resistant to wear over time. He said the company can represent five years of use, or even more, within a couple of weeks of testing.

Article Title: Meta's 'highest-paid' employee Alexandr Wang says sorry for ‘dumb joke’ after CTO tech company says he booked ticket through Muse AI agent
Article Text:
Meta's chief AI officer Alexander Wang

What is Meta Muse

Alexandr Wang, recognised as Meta’s highest-paid employee, issued a quick lighthearted apology on social media platform X (formerly Twitter) after making a playful remark to a tech executive who used the company's autonomous AI agent, Muse, to arrange air travel. The exchange unfolded when WebFlow CTO Utkarsh Sengar posted publicly about testing the capabilities of Meta’s AI tool to handle flight logistics.“Just booked plane tickets via Muse. Never going back,” Sengar shared online, praising the workflow of the reservation process. Responding to the post, Wang initially celebrated the milestone before offering a humorous piece of travel advice:“Awesome!!!” Wang replied, adding “But also i probably would recommend booking a return flight and going home at some point (sorry dumb joke).”Earlier this month, Meta launched an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, Muse, capable of executing tasks such as sending emails, listing a car for sale and booking travel. With Muse, CEO Mark Zuckerberg aims to deliver “personal superintelligence” across Meta's global platform. In a post on X, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote, “Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you.”Initially limited to US users, Muse will operate through a standalone app and within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. The company that for now, Muse launches on iOS, Android and the web, with free and paid tiers, and support for AI glasses coming soon.Based on the open-source OpenClaw framework, Muse functions by linking directly to a user’s calendar, email, financial services, smart home hardware and health platforms. The company said that users must manually grant permissions for each service and the model allows them to revoke access at any point.As per the company, each Muse instance runs within an isolated, cloud-based virtual machine designed to emulate an individual personal computer. This architecture allows the software to execute long-running tasks autonomously in the background without requiring continuous user interaction.
Article Summary: Alexandr wang, meta's chief ai officer, issued a lighthearted apology on social media platform x (formerly twitter) wang was responding to a tech executive who used the company's autonomous ai agent, muse, to arrange air travel. The exchange unfolded when webflow cto utkarsh sengar posted publicly about testing the capabilities of meta's ai tool.

Article Title: Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report
Article Text:
Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report

Will Apple Pay support UPI in India

Apple Pay has been in talks with Indian banks

Apple Pay could finally launch in India as early as October, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Gurman said Apple is preparing to launch Apple Pay in India “finally” next month. The service is expected to support card payments, while there are also reports that Apple could bring UPI support to the platform. The service was first launched in the US in 2014.Gurman said Apple Pay is expected to support UPI alongside card payments. UPI is India's widely used digital payments system and allows users to make instant payments through participating banks and apps. However, Reuters' recent report about Apple's India plans did not mention UPI as part of the initial rollout.Earlier reports had also suggested that Apple Pay could initially launch without UPI, with support potentially added later.According to Reuters, Axis Bank is expected to be Apple's first major banking partner when Apple Pay launches in India. Apple is reportedly preparing to support Axis Bank credit cards initially. The company is also in discussions with HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, although commercial agreements with those lenders had not been finalised, according to the report.Apple is expected to add more banks over time through separate agreements with lenders.Apple has reportedly been discussing its India plans with several major banks and payment networks for months. A Bloomberg report in February said Apple was in talks with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, as well as Visa and Mastercard. At the time, Apple Pay was expected to launch around the middle of 2026, but that timeline did not happen.If the latest October timeline is accurate, Apple Pay could soon enter India's established digital payments market, initially with limited banking support before expanding to more lenders.
Article Summary: Apple pay could launch in india as early as october, according to bloomberg. The service is expected to support card payments, while there are also reports that apple could bring upi support to the platform. Apple has been in talks with indian banks and payment networks for months.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
Article Text:
A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. Article Title: Four sisters started a Thai-inspired popcorn brand after a family trip; it now makes $7,000 a month
Article Text:
Image: Courtesy of Party Of. The Lertlumprasert sisters

How a trip to Thailand inspired the Lertlumprasert sisters' popcorn brand

Launching Party Of: branding investment and early recipe development

A production crisis during Compass Group's Retail Incubator Program

Party Of's growth and the sisters' advice for other founders

The Lertlumprasert sisters, Lisa, Lita, Charlene and Charlie, had talked about starting a business together since childhood. That idea finally took shape in February 2023, after a family trip to Thailand left them with a suitcase full of snacks their American friends loved. Combined with their frustration over the "better-for-you" snack options available in the US, the trip inspired their Thai-inspired popcorn brand, Party Of. Here's how the Washington, DC-based sisters built the business from a homemade batch into a side hustle generating steady monthly revenue.According to Lita, a data scientist, the sisters had returned from visiting family in Thailand with an abundance of Thai snacks to share with friends, who loved everything they brought back. As reported by Entrepreneur, what experience, paired with the sisters' shared sense that healthier snack options in the US weren't inspiring, led them to take classic, accessible snack foods and give them their own signature spin. Lisa, who owns and operates Thai restaurants, brought culinary experience to the idea, while Lita's data science background, Charlene's UX design skills and Charlie's product management expertise rounded out the founding team behind what would become Party Of.To get the business off the ground, the sisters began by defining what Charlie, a product manager, called the six dimensions of product-market fit, target customer, problem, value proposition, competitive advantage, growth strategy and business model. Identifying branding as a key competitive advantage, they invested $28,000 to work with branding agency Outline. Recipe development and inventory costs stayed low early on, since Lisa used ingredients already available at her restaurant, bought corn and brown bags, and applied a "ZingPop" sticker, later rebranded Party Of, that Charlene designed on Canva. The StartupCPG Slack group later became an invaluable free resource for learning and connecting with other CPG entrepreneurs.The sisters' biggest challenge came during their participation in Compass Group's Retail Incubator Program, which required them to produce over 30,000 units in under four months, more than they had sold in total during the seven months since launching. To hit that number, the team had to switch to a new pillow-pouch format entirely, which meant reworking the packaging design, getting up to speed on material compositions, and bringing on a different co-packer once their existing setup couldn't handle the equipment or scale required. Things didn't go smoothly from there either, bags weren't cutting cleanly on the production line, shipments got stuck at customs, and tariffs added another unexpected hit. The sisters got through it the way they'd gotten through everything else so far, calling on people in their network and trusting their best judgment even without all the answers.By 2025, Party Of's revenue had grown fourfold from the year before, and the sisters trimmed their cost of goods sold by roughly a quarter, numbers Lisa points to as proof the harder years of building the brand are starting to pay off. Monthly revenue now sits at a fairly steady $7,000, though every so often a bigger order comes through, anywhere from $5,000 to $50,000, on top of that baseline. For Charlene, the payoff isn't just financial; having full say over every decision is a kind of satisfaction she never got from a corporate role. Lisa's advice to anyone starting echoes how they began, nail down product-market fit before anything else, because that early clarity spares you from wasted effort later. Charlene's one regret, if she's honest, is not treating the books seriously sooner.

The washington, dc-based sisters built the business from a homemade batch into a side hustle generating steady monthly revenue.
